report:
**Conclusion:** Your claim is well supported, with an important qualification: tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) is an *addition to*, not a replacement for, prompt newborn hepatitis-B vaccination (and HBIG where available).

The rationale is strong: high maternal HBV DNA is the principal predictor of transmission despite infant immunoprophylaxis. A pivotal Chinese randomized trial found that TDF begun at 30–32 weeks in highly viremic mothers substantially lowered infant HBV infection compared with no maternal antiviral treatment. This evidence underlies recommendations to offer TDF to HBsAg-positive pregnant people with HBV DNA ≥200,000 IU/mL (or, in some settings, positive HBeAg), generally late in the second/early in the third trimester.

Evidence is not completely uniform. A large double-blind Thai trial starting TDF at 28 weeks found no statistically significant incremental benefit over placebo. However, transmission was already exceptionally rare in both groups—likely because newborn vaccine and HBIG were given very rapidly after birth—so it had limited ability to demonstrate an additional benefit. That result supports the central importance of high-quality infant prophylaxis, rather than showing TDF is ineffective in the higher-risk real-world settings that motivated the recommendation.

WHO retained its recommendation for maternal TDF prophylaxis in women with HBV DNA ≥200,000 IU/mL. TDF also has substantial pregnancy safety experience, though postpartum liver tests matter because stopping therapy can be followed by hepatitis flares.

Clinical decisions should include HBV-DNA measurement, assessment of whether the mother independently needs long-term HBV treatment, infant birth-dose vaccination/HBIG planning, and postpartum follow-up.
